title: Last Rays

image.credit: Musée des beaux-arts de Quimper, France; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A landscape with trees and the light of the sun low in the sky, as the title Last Rays suggests. The painting is an oil on canvas from 1911 and shows woods and the glow of a sunrise or sunset.

source.museum: Musée des beaux-arts de Quimper, France
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting on canvas by Félix Vallotton, made in 1911 and now in the Musée des beaux-arts de Quimper in France. The page labels it Nabi and tags it with woods, forests and trees and with sunrise and sunset.

descriptions.k: This painting is called Last Rays. It shows trees and the light of the sun. Look for the trees. Look for the place where the light is strongest. What time of day do you think it is?
descriptions.g12: Félix Vallotton painted Last Rays in 1911. The title means the last bits of sunlight before the day ends. The painting shows trees and a glowing sky. Look closely at the trees and the light. How do they make the picture feel quiet or calm? Tell a partner what you notice.
descriptions.g35: Félix Vallotton painted Last Rays in 1911 with oil on canvas. The title points to the final light of the day, and the painting is tagged with woods, trees and sunset. Look closely at how the trees and the glow of the sun share the picture. What mood does this time of day create, and which details make you think so?
descriptions.g68: Vallotton's Last Rays (1911) belongs to the Nabi group, French artists who favored bold, simplified design over exact copying of nature. The title names the last light of day, and the page tags the painting with trees and sunset. How might the painter use trees and light to suggest a moment passing? Point to details you can see as evidence.
descriptions.g910: Vallotton painted Last Rays in 1911, and its title, tags (woods, trees, sunrise and sunset) and Nabi label suggest a landscape built around fading light. Nabi artists often stressed design and flat areas of color over realistic detail. How could the arrangement of trees and the glow of the sky express a mood and not just record a place? Consider more than one reading.
descriptions.g1112: Last Rays (1911) is by Félix Vallotton, who is associated with the Nabis, artists who treated a picture as a designed surface and not a window onto nature. A landscape titled for the last light of day invites readings of time, ending and mood, though the title alone cannot settle meaning. How do the trees, the sky and the title together shape an interpretation, and how would you weigh competing readings?

k.daily: Find the trees in Last Rays. How many can you count?
k.emotion: How does this painting make you feel, sleepy, calm or excited? Point to what makes you feel that way.
k.observation: Point to the brightest part of the painting. What do you see there?
k.analysis: Which is bigger in this painting, the trees or the sun? Point to show me.
k.line: Trace a tall tree with your finger. Does your finger go up, down or sideways?
k.shape: Look at the trees and the sky. What shapes can you find?
k.color: Which color do you see the most in Last Rays? Point to it.
k.texture: Paint can look smooth or bumpy. Which parts of this painting look smooth to you?
k.space: Which tree looks closest to you? Which looks far away?
k.light: Where is the sunlight coming from in this painting?
k.meaning: The painting is called Last Rays. What do you think the painter wanted to show?
k.culture: The painter lived in France long ago. What would you see outside at the end of the day where you live?
k.technique: The painter used oil paint on cloth called canvas. What tool do you think he used to put paint on it?
k.personal: Where would you like to stand in this painting? Tell us why.
k.critical: If this painting had a different name, what would you call it?

g12.daily: The title is Last Rays. What do you see in the painting that fits that name?
g12.emotion: What kind of mood does the end of the day have in this painting? Tell a partner which parts make you think so.
g12.observation: List three things you notice about the trees and three things you notice about the light.
g12.analysis: Why do you think the painter put the trees where he did in Last Rays?
g12.line: How do the lines of the tree trunks and branches move across the painting?
g12.shape: Which shapes in the trees repeat? How do they make the painting feel organized?
g12.color: Which colors make the painting feel like the end of a day? Show a partner where you see them.
g12.texture: How did the painter make the leaves and the sky look different from each other?
g12.space: How can you tell which parts of the woods are near and which are far?
g12.light: Where is the light brightest, and where is it darker? What does that tell you about the sun?
g12.meaning: Why might a painter choose to paint the last light of the day?
g12.culture: Vallotton made this in 1911. What do you think a walk in the woods was like for people then?
g12.technique: Oil paint is thick and slow to dry. How might that help a painter show glowing light?
g12.personal: Think of a time you watched the sun go down. How is your memory like or different from this painting?
g12.critical: What would change in the painting if the same woods were shown at noon?

g35.daily: What clues in the painting tell you it shows the end of a day and not the middle?
g35.emotion: How does the light of sunset or sunrise shape the mood of Last Rays? Use details from the painting.
g35.observation: Describe how the trees and the sun are placed in relation to each other in the painting.
g35.analysis: How does Vallotton balance the dark shapes of the trees with the bright light of the sky?
g35.line: How do the vertical lines of the trees affect the way your eyes travel across the painting?
g35.shape: Are the trees drawn as detailed shapes or simple ones? How does that choice change the feeling of the painting?
g35.color: How do warm and cool colors in the painting work together to show the fading light?
g35.texture: Does the painted surface look rough, smooth or both? What might that tell you about how he painted?
g35.space: How does the painter create the feeling that the woods go back into the distance?
g35.light: How does the low sun change the way the trees look compared with in full daylight?
g35.meaning: The page tags this work with sunrise and sunset. Why might the title Last Rays push you toward sunset?
g35.culture: Vallotton belonged to a group called the Nabis. What do you think a group of artists gains from working together?
g35.technique: What choices does a painter make when using oil paint to show glowing light?
g35.personal: What place near you would you paint at the end of the day, and why?
g35.critical: How could two viewers look at the same painting and feel different things? Give an example from Last Rays.

g68.daily: Which single detail in Last Rays best supports the idea of a day coming to an end, and why?
g68.emotion: How might the balance of light and shadow create a feeling of calm, sadness or hope? Choose one and defend it.
g68.observation: Compare the treatment of the sky with the treatment of the trees. What differences in paint handling do you notice?
g68.analysis: How does the placement of the trees frame the light and shape where a viewer looks first?
g68.line: How do the edges of the trunks and the horizon work together to structure the composition?
g68.shape: Nabi artists favored simplified forms. Where does Vallotton simplify the shapes of trees, and what does that do for the mood?
g68.color: How does the color scheme push the painting away from a realistic copy of nature?
g68.texture: How does the paint surface contribute to the feeling of evening air and light?
g68.space: How does overlapping and changing value suggest depth in the woods?
g68.light: What does the direction of the light suggest about where the sun is, and how does it shape the objects it touches?
g68.meaning: Why might an artist choose a quiet landscape to suggest the passing of time instead of showing people?
g68.culture: In 1911, many French artists were moving away from strictly realistic landscapes. How does Last Rays reflect that?
g68.technique: Why would oil paint suit a subject based on glowing, changing light?
g68.personal: How does this painting compare with a sunset or sunrise you have seen yourself?
g68.critical: The title tells us the subject. How does knowing the title help or limit your reading? Support your answer with the painting.

g910.daily: How does the combination of the title and the visual evidence direct you toward an interpretation of Last Rays?
g910.emotion: What emotional register does the fading-light subject suggest, and which formal choices carry it?
g910.observation: Choose a small area of the painting and describe the brushwork, color and edges you see there.
g910.analysis: How does Vallotton organize the relationship between the vertical forms of the trees and the field of light?
g910.line: How do contour and edge, as opposed to modeled shading, shape the painting's design?
g910.shape: How might the Nabi emphasis on flat, simplified shapes appear in the trees and the glow of the sky?
g910.color: How does color function expressively here, rather than descriptively, and what evidence supports that?
g910.texture: How does surface handling differentiate air, foliage and ground, or does it unify them?
g910.space: To what degree does the painting build depth, and where does it flatten space into pattern?
g910.light: How does the painter convey the quality of low sunlight, and how does it affect the legibility of forms?
g910.meaning: How might a landscape stand for time and mortality without including any figures? Consider the evidence.
g910.culture: How does a Nabi approach to landscape differ from the Impressionist goal of recording an effect of light?
g910.technique: How could working in oil on canvas allow a painter to adjust and layer tones in a sunset subject?
g910.personal: What does it mean for you to look at a painting of an ordinary place at the end of the day?
g910.critical: How reliable is a title as evidence of an artist's intention, and how does Last Rays test that?

g1112.daily: What interpretive claim about time and nature would you make for Last Rays, and what evidence would carry it?
g1112.emotion: How does the work balance contemplation and melancholy, and which formal means create that tension?
g1112.observation: Which detail resists a simple sunset reading, and how would you account for it?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional structure of trees and light reflect the Nabi conception of the picture as a designed surface?
g1112.line: How does the emphasis on edge and silhouette over modeling affect the painting's decorative and expressive qualities?
g1112.shape: How do simplified, large-scale forms participate in an expressive reduction of landscape?
g1112.color: In what ways might color here be understood as symbolic or psychological and not naturalistic?
g1112.texture: How does the interplay between painted surface and depicted space inform your reading of the work as an object?
g1112.space: How does the painter negotiate between illusion of depth and the flatness of the canvas, and to what end?
g1112.light: How does the representation of waning light function as both a visual subject and a metaphor?
g1112.meaning: How might you argue for and against reading the title Last Rays as a statement about endings?
g1112.culture: How does the painting situate itself between nineteenth-century landscape traditions and early twentieth-century modernism?
g1112.technique: What does the choice of oil on canvas, a long-standing medium, suggest about the painter's relation to tradition?
g1112.personal: How does your own experience of dusk or dawn shape the assumptions you bring to this painting?
g1112.critical: What kinds of external information about Vallotton's life and period would strengthen or complicate your reading, and why?

safety.method: Title, year (1911), medium (oil on canvas), collection (Musée des beaux-arts de Quimper), movement label (Nabi), tags (Woods, Forests, & Trees; Sunrise & Sunset) and the public-domain statement were read from the arthistoryproject.com page text. teacherNote.context: An oil painting made in 1911 by Félix Vallotton, now in the Musée des beaux-arts de Quimper in France. The page labels it Nabi and tags it with trees and sunrise or sunset.
directions: Have students look for two minutes in silence, then list what they see before reading the title aloud. Ask how the title changes what they notice.
Ask students to draw a tree-and-sky scene using only a few large shapes and two or three colors, as a way to explore simplified design.
Discuss with older students how a title can guide interpretation, and where a painting might support more than one reading.
